visuals.title: Where it starts
visuals.text: Dopamine-making neurons in the substantia nigra die, starving the basal ganglia of dopamine.

glossary.Neurodegenerative: Describes diseases where nerve cells progressively die and are not replaced.
glossary.Dopamine: Chemical messenger the basal ganglia need for smooth, quick movement.
glossary.Dopaminergic neurons: Nerve cells that make and release dopamine.
glossary.Resting tremor: Tremor present when the limb is relaxed and supported, easing with movement.
glossary.Postural instability: Poor balance and tendency to fall, especially when turning or pushed.
glossary.Shuffling gait: Walking with short steps and feet barely leaving the floor.
glossary.Stooped posture: Forward-bent posture of the head and trunk.
glossary.Autonomic dysfunction: Failure of the automatic nervous system, causing constipation, postural hypotension and bladder problems.
glossary.Olfactory loss: Reduced or lost sense of smell.
glossary.Motor fluctuations: Swings between good mobility and stiffness or slowness as levodopa levels rise and fall.
glossary.Drug-induced parkinsonism: Parkinson-like signs caused by dopamine-blocking drugs, usually symmetrical.
glossary.Postural hypotension: A fall in blood pressure on standing, causing dizziness or falls.
glossary.Dopamine antagonists: Drugs that block dopamine receptors, such as antipsychotics and some antiemetics.
glossary.Prochlorperazine: Dopamine-blocking anti-sickness drug that worsens Parkinson's.
glossary.Droperidol: Dopamine-blocking antiemetic and sedative that worsens Parkinson's.
glossary.Dopamine transporter: Protein on dopamine neurons that recycles dopamine; reduced on DaTSCAN when neurons are lost.
glossary.Peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor: Stops levodopa turning into dopamine outside the brain, reducing nausea and letting more reach the brain.
glossary.Athetosis: Slow, writhing involuntary movements, usually of the hands and feet.
glossary.Pramipexole: Oral dopamine agonist used in Parkinson's.
glossary.Apomorphine: Injected dopamine agonist used for severe off periods.
glossary.Selegiline: MAO-B inhibitor that slows dopamine breakdown in the brain.
glossary.Rasagiline: MAO-B inhibitor that slows dopamine breakdown in the brain.
glossary.Transdermal: Given through the skin as a patch.
glossary.Polypharmacy: Taking many medicines at once, raising the risk of interactions and side effects.
glossary.Occupational therapy: Therapy helping people manage daily activities, often with aids and adaptations.
glossary.Parkinsonian crisis: Sudden severe worsening of rigidity and immobility, often after missed medication.
glossary.Antiemetic: A drug that prevents or treats nausea and vomiting.
glossary.Blood-brain barrier: A tight lining of brain blood vessels that keeps many drugs out of the brain.
glossary.Psychosis: Loss of contact with reality, such as hallucinations or delusions.
glossary.Rapid tranquillisation: Giving sedating medicine quickly to calm a dangerously agitated patient.
glossary.Direct pathway: Basal ganglia route that facilitates wanted movement; driven by dopamine.
glossary.Indirect pathway: Basal ganglia route that inhibits unwanted movement; dopamine normally restrains it.
glossary.Pulsatile: Rising and falling in bursts rather than steady.
glossary.Movement disorder specialist: A neurologist with expertise in conditions such as Parkinson's and tremor.
